Chapter 6: The Long Shadow of Trauma and the Struggle for Normalcy
You know, there’s a peculiar ache that tends to linger long after chaos has faded—a kind of invisible weight that follows survivors into every new day. For those who grew up as children in the midst of war, stepping outside the rehabilitation center felt both familiar and strangely foreign.
Imagine walking down streets that once rang with laughter, but now seem haunted by memories. Just going to the market, or sitting in a classroom, could trigger a rush of images: flashes of gunfire, pounding footsteps, the faces of friends and family lost along the way.
There’s one young man who comes to mind. He’d just left the center, trying to settle into a relative’s home in the city. All he wanted was to blend in—to be just another student. But his past clung to him. At night, he’d jolt awake in a cold sweat, heart racing, sure he was back in the bush.
And during the day, focusing on lessons felt impossible. His mind kept drifting back to the rules of survival he’d learned as a child soldier. The world around him expected him to move on, but deep down, his body and mind were still fighting their own battles.
Most people didn’t really get it. They saw a quiet, withdrawn teenager and figured he was just shy, or maybe stubborn. Hardly anyone realized that every loud noise, every argument, even a sudden touch, could send him spiraling. He wanted to explain how he felt, but the words were just too heavy, too tangled to share.
And that’s when it hit him: the hardest part of recovery wasn’t surviving the war—it was surviving the peace that came after.
Some days, the urge to run was overwhelming. The city felt crowded and unpredictable. Oddly enough, he missed the camaraderie of his old group, even though it had been born out of violence. The loneliness was sharp—a constant reminder that while the world had moved on, he was still stuck in the past.
But then, there were these small, almost hidden moments of hope. A teacher who actually listened. A neighbor’s warm smile. A classmate inviting him for a game of soccer after school. Sure, these gestures didn’t erase the pain, but they made it a little more bearable.
The struggle for normalcy was, and still is, ongoing. There were setbacks—days when memories flooded back, when anger or sadness just bubbled over. But there was also progress. He learned to spot the signs of a panic attack, and started asking for help when he needed it.
He discovered that healing isn’t about forgetting. It’s about learning to live with the memories. The past would always be a part of him, but it didn’t have to define his future.
And for so many survivors, the journey looked a lot like this. The world expected them to pick up where they left off, but the war had changed everything. The real challenge wasn’t just surviving—it was finding a way to thrive in a world that no longer made sense.
It’s a slow, and sometimes painful process. But every small victory—a good night’s sleep, a passing grade, a new friend—each one is a step toward reclaiming a life that was interrupted by war.
